prompts:
This is an instructional notebook. It is notebook 7, the last notebook of part 2 (classification) of the course "Tabular Foundation Models with TabICL".

Content: same fraud setup and costs as TabICL_calibration (10,000 rows, 10 `StratifiedShuffleSplit` splits of 1,500 training and 500 test rows). The business metric sums the gains of each decision and depends on each transaction's amount, so the notebook enables metadata routing (`sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)`), builds a scorer with `make_scorer` and `set_score_request(amount=True)`, and passes `params={"amount": amount}` to `cross_validate`. Blocking is the positive class. Baselines: 'always accept' (`DummyClassifier` predicting 0) loses about 3,000 euros on the first test set and on every split, because frauds are 5 percent of our rows against 0.17 percent in the full dataset; euros here only compare models and thresholds and do not estimate a bank's earnings. 'Always reject' loses even more; an oracle earns about 780 euros per test set. The notebook keeps only predicted probabilities, not fitted models, to save memory (a remark that applies to the local package).

Results of the reference run: at the default threshold, both models close about 80 percent of the gap between 'always accept' and the oracle, gradient boosting earning about 160 euros per test set and TabICL about 220, with standard deviations of about 400. Gain curves across log-spaced thresholds: gradient boosting's nearly binary probabilities give slowly varying curves (about 160 at 0.5 to 260 at 0.001); TabICL's curves have a plateau between about 2 and 50 percent, highest around 3 to 5 percent, and fall steeply below 1 percent because TabICL gives legitimate payments small but honest risks. Best gains read on the test sets are optimistic. The rule from the costs again earns about 150 more than the default for TabICL and about 50 more for gradient boosting.

`TunedThresholdClassifierCV` (internal cross-validation on the training rows, business scorer, log-spaced thresholds, `cv=3`, `store_cv_results=True`, amounts routed to its internal folds) picks thresholds from 0.02 to 57 percent for gradient boosting and from 1.6 to 64 percent for TabICL. Tuning does not pay off: about as much as the default for TabICL, about 30 less for gradient boosting, and less than the rule from the costs for both. Applying each picked threshold to all test sets, and subtracting the rule's gain per test set, shows that no single threshold beats the rule for TabICL on a typical test set. Key lesson: a tuned threshold only depends on the ranking, so calibration matters less once we tune; calibration still gives a threshold without data, avoids a risky draw from about 25 frauds per validation fold, and allows a threshold per amount.

Variability: the standard deviation is about twice the mean gains, mostly from frauds that slip through (a 1,000 euro fraud needs 50,000 euros of legitimate payments to win back). Large frauds such as one of 723 euros in split 5 explain most of the rule's gain for TabICL. Per-split differences show the two models make almost the same decisions at the default threshold; neither is reliably more profitable, and the clearest result is that TabICL's calibrated probabilities make the free rule beat tuning.

Place in the course: last notebook of the course. Related scikit-learn course material: tuning the decision threshold and classification metrics (Evaluating Model Performance), baselines with `DummyClassifier`.
